raw_evidence.quote: table "users" { schema = schema.public column "id" { type = int } primary_key { columns = [column.id] } }
A `primary_key` is a child resource of a `table`, and it defines the table's primary key
column "manager_id" { type = int } ... foreign_key "manager_fk" { columns = [column.manager_id] ref_columns = [column.id]
A `check` is a child resource of a `table` that describes a `CHECK` constraint. table "products" { column "price" { type = float } check "positive price" { expr = "price > 0" } }
In some cases, an Atlas DDL document may contain multiple tables of the same name. This usually happens when the same table name appears in two different schemas.
table "a" "users" ... table "b" "users" ... referencing different schemas, with foreign keys using table.public.users.column.id syntax
Columns include type and optional attributes like `null`, `default`, and `comment`.

composite_primary_key.rationale: The `columns` attribute of `primary_key` is a plain HCL list of column references with no documented cardinality limit; the identical list-typed pattern is shown for `index.columns` with an implied multi-entry use. No literal 2+-column example was captured in this fetch, so this is read directly off the grammar shape, not a worked example.

multiple_self_referencing_foreign_keys_o.rationale: Each `foreign_key` block is an independently named child resource of `table`; the documented single self-referencing example (`manager_id` -> `column.id` on the same table) demonstrates the mechanism. Because blocks are named and repeatable, nothing in the retrieved text restricts a table to one such block, so three distinctly named self-referencing foreign_key blocks on one table follow directly from the grammar. No literal 3-simultaneous-self-FK example was found; this is an extrapolation from a 1-self-FK example plus the general repeatable/named-block pattern.

nullable_foreign_key.citation: §Column ('optional attributes like `null`, `default`, and `comment`') combined with §Foreign Key
nullable_foreign_key.rationale: A foreign_key's referencing column is an ordinary table column, and columns carry a `null` attribute per the column-attributes text; nothing suggests FK-bearing columns are exempted from that attribute.

multi_column_unique_constraint.rationale: Same list-typed `columns` attribute as `primary_key`; the captured example shows one column, so a 2-column unique index is inferred from the list-typed attribute rather than a literal worked example.

one_to_zero_or_one_relationship.citation: No relationship/cardinality keyword found in §Schema, §Table, §Primary Key, §Foreign Key, §Index, §Check, or §Table Qualification
one_to_zero_or_one_relationship.rationale: Atlas HCL is a physical schema language: the retrieved sections define schema, table, column, primary_key, foreign_key, index, and check — there is no block or attribute expressing relationship cardinality as a first-class concept. A one-to-zero-or-one relationship must be reconstructed by a reader from two independently documented primitives — a nullable foreign_key column plus a unique index on that same column — rather than declared directly. This absence claim is based on the sections retrieved in this fetch, not an exhaustive read of the entire hcl documentation tree.

several_logical_schemas_in_one_database.citation: §Table Qualification — multiple `schema` blocks in one document, tables qualified per schema, cross-schema FK via `table.<schema>.<table>.column.<col>`
several_logical_schemas_in_one_database.rationale: Directly documented: the page describes multiple schemas coexisting in one HCL document, with a naming-qualification mechanism and a worked cross-schema foreign-key reference syntax.
